catalog_citation: Gustafsson, Maria. 2026. Tone in Mulgi of Chad: the first description of verbal & nominal tone in Mulgi [mvh], a Chadic East A language with typologically rare tonal phenomena. MA thesis (Linguistics), Trinity Western University, Langley BC. xvii+247 pp. (264 pp.). Supervisor B. Yoder; committee K. Snider, W. Gardner. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.
catalog_locator: sec. 7.1 Summary, pp. 165-166; stress remark sec. 2.3.2, p. 15; see also Abstract p. vi and sec. 5.4.6 (H raising), p. 100
catalog_quote: The results of the tone analysis (Chapters 5 and 6) showed that tone is contrastive in both the verb and noun systems, with two active tones (L and H) creating five tone patterns (Ø, L, HL, H, LH) realized at four different pitch levels (low, mid, high, super high). [...] The syllable profile of simple verbs and nouns was not found to affect the pitch realization of tone patterns, instead, the syllable is the TBU. [...] [p.15] Nevertheless, since no clear sign of stress has been observed to impact tone (though questions on some vowel changes remain), it is considered beyond the scope of this thesis.

new_statements.relation_note: Full first-hand tone description (chapters 5-6) plus segmental phonology overview (ch. 4); explicit remark that stress was not observed to affect tone and is out of scope.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mulgi is a tone language: two underlying tones (L, H), five lexical/grammatical tone patterns on morphemes (toneless, L, H, LH, HL), four surface pitch levels (low, mid, high, super-high), syllable = tone-bearing unit; toneless morphemes receive default mid pitch; numerous tonal processes (H raising, H copying, L spreading, fusion, LHL simplification). No word-stress system is described; the author reports no clear sign of stress interacting with tone and leaves stress/metrical structure outside the scope.
new_statements.exceptions: p.100 (sec. 5.4.6): location of H raising on penultimate syllables unexplained; author checked intensity curves and found no correlation with raised H, but perfective Stem2 shows higher intensity on its second syllable than the first, 'This could be related to stress or simply the inherent amplitude of different vowel qualities. This deserves further investigation.' Prepositions only L; no HL suffix/enclitic observed; tonal interaction across word boundaries rare.
new_statements.identity_note: Explicitly Mulgi [mvh] (keywords 'Mulgi, Mire'), Chadic East A, subgroup A.1.1 with Ndam, Somrai, Tumak; Tandjile region, Chad; author is the SIL Tchad fieldworker who edited the 2020 Mulgi primer; data = 8,500+ recordings collected in Chad 2024 after fieldwork 2019-2022. Not the South-Estonian Mulgi dialect.

Gustafsson 2026:7 cites it together with Roberts 2018 as the only existing manuscripts on Mulgi and only for open segmental questions (central vowels [ɨ ə a], the liquids [r l ɽ], phonemic status of [ɗ]); p. 23 cites Weiss (2013) for the suggestion that [ɽ] might be an amalgam of [ŋl]. The thesis presents itself as the first description of Mulgi tone, so any tone content in the esquisse is at most a preliminary tone inventory/transcription.
